title: Understand legal principles relevant to marketing within the seed industry

lessons.title: Contracts in seed marketing
lessons.html:
Contracts in seed marketing

Every sale of seed is a contract, whether it is a written agreement with a large co-op or a farmer buying ten bags over the counter. People who market seed must understand basic contract principles so that they make agreements that are valid, fair and enforceable.

Requirements for a valid contract in South African law

  • Agreement (consensus): both parties agree on the same terms, usually through an offer and acceptance.
  • Capacity: the parties are legally able to contract, for example adults of sound mind, or a person authorised to sign for a company or co-op.
  • Legality: the contract is not against the law, for example it may not be for selling seed of an unregistered cultivar where registration is required.
  • Possibility: it must be possible to perform.
  • Formalities: some contracts must be in writing or signed; follow company policy and put important agreements in writing.

Common contracts in the seed business

ContractExample
Sale agreementInvoice and terms and conditions for seed sold
Credit agreementAccount terms or harvest credit to a farmer
Distribution or dealer agreementA co-op that sells the company's seed
Licence agreementRights to sell a protected cultivar
Seed production contractA contract grower producing seed

Terms and conditions

Seed companies usually include standard terms on invoices and labels, for example limits on liability because field results depend on weather and management. Such terms must be brought to the customer's attention and must be fair. A sales representative must not make verbal promises, such as guaranteed yields, that go against the written terms. Such promises can bind the company and lead to disputes.

When in doubt about a contract, ask your manager or the company's legal adviser before signing or promising.

lessons.title: Laws that affect how seed is marketed
lessons.html:
Laws that affect how seed is marketed

Several laws control what seed may be sold, how it must be labelled and how it may be advertised. A marketer who breaks them can expose the company to fines, court cases and loss of reputation.

Seed-specific laws

  • Plant Improvement Act 53 of 1976: controls the sale of seed of many crops, including cultivar listing, quality standards, labelling and certification. Only seed meeting the prescribed standards and properly labelled may be sold.
  • Plant Breeders' Rights Act 15 of 1976: gives breeders exclusive rights to protected cultivars. Others may not multiply or sell such seed without authorisation. Marketers must never encourage farmers to save and sell protected seed illegally.
  • Genetically Modified Organisms Act 15 of 1997: controls the use and release of GM crops. Only approved GM events may be marketed, and conditions such as refuge requirements for insect-resistant crops must be communicated to farmers.
  • Act 36 of 1947: controls agricultural remedies, including seed treatment chemicals and their labelling.

General trade laws

  • Consumer Protection Act 68 of 2008: protects consumers against misleading marketing and unfair terms, and gives rights to safe, good-quality goods. Small buyers such as home gardeners and many smallholders are covered; some large businesses fall outside its scope.
  • Competition Act 89 of 1998: prohibits practices such as price fixing between competitors and abuse of a dominant position.
  • Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA): controls how customer information is collected, used and protected, including direct marketing by SMS or e-mail.
  • National Credit Act 34 of 2005: may apply when credit is given to individuals.

Practical rules for marketers

  • Make only claims you can prove with trial data.
  • Use correct cultivar names and label information.
  • Never agree prices or divide areas with competitors.
  • Get consent before sending direct marketing messages where required.
  • Keep records of agreements and customer communication.

lessons.title: Applying legal principles in daily marketing
lessons.html:
Applying legal principles in daily marketing

Legal principles are only useful if they are applied in everyday work. Below are situations a seed marketer may meet, with the legal issue and the correct response.

Case examples

SituationLegal issueCorrect response
A farmer asks you to promise 10 t/ha if he buys a hybridMisleading claims; binding verbal promiseShare real trial data for his area; explain yield depends on rain and management
A competitor's rep suggests both companies keep prices up this seasonPrice fixing under the Competition ActRefuse, end the conversation and report it to your manager
A grower offers to sell you saved seed of a protected cultivar cheaplyPlant Breeders' Rights infringementRefuse and report it
You want to SMS a promotion to a list bought from a third partyPOPIA and direct marketing consentCheck consent rules with your manager first
A co-op wants extra discount in exchange for not stocking a competitorPossible competition law concernRefer to your manager or legal adviser

Handling disputes

Disputes may arise over quality, delivery, payment or contract terms. Try to resolve them through discussion first, using evidence such as laboratory results, delivery notes and the signed contract. If this fails, the company may use mediation, arbitration or court action, depending on the contract. Never threaten a customer; refer serious disputes to management.

Ethics

Not everything legal is ethical. Treating small and emerging farmers fairly, explaining products in a language they understand and not exploiting their lack of information builds long-term trust and a good name for the company and the industry.

Key points

  • A valid contract needs agreement, capacity, legality and possibility, with required formalities.
  • Verbal promises can bind the company; avoid guaranteeing results.
  • Seed laws control cultivar listing, labelling, certification, breeders' rights and GM crops.
  • Consumer, competition and privacy laws govern how seed is marketed.
  • Refuse illegal requests and refer legal questions to your manager.
